_comment: Shared cross-language corpus for the eight social columns (PSY-1997).
THE CONTRACT: anything the Go write boundary stores must be renderable by
the frontend read gate. Nothing may be storable and unrenderable without
being named in storableButUnrenderable below, or a curator's save silently
produces no link and nobody can see why.
Go reads this file in utils.TestSocialLinkCorpus; TypeScript reads the same
file in frontend/lib/socialLinks.test.ts. Both assert their own half plus
the host table itself, so a field, a host or a rule added to one language
and not the other fails the other language's suite and names the value. A
rule the corpus carries no case for is a rule it cannot police, so add
cases with rules.
platforms  = the anchored fields and their host bases. Each side asserts
its own table equals this, which is what stops the two lists
drifting.
unanchored = the fields that make no platform claim and accept any host.
handleBases = where a bare handle resolves on each field that takes one.
A field absent from it takes no handle. Both sides assert
their own table equals this, because a base is not covered
by the anchor assertions: a typo in one still produces an
ANCHORED url, and would send every legacy handle to the
wrong page while every other assertion passed.
storable   = the write boundary accepts it AND the reader must render it.
storableButUnrenderable = the write boundary accepts it and the reader
renders nothing, each row's `why` saying which reason: the
browser's URL parser refuses the value outright, or the reader
refuses it deliberately. Every one fails closed (no link), and
pinning them here is what keeps the gap written down instead
of merely true.
A blank or whitespace-only value is in no bucket: it is the clear-the-field
gesture, which both sides read as no value rather than as a link, and the
unit tests on each side cover it.
refusedByWriter = the write boundary refuses it. `rendersAnyway` marks the
legacy shapes the reader deliberately keeps: handles and
scheme-less domains that still land on the platform. The rest
are the ones a click would carry off-platform, and the reader
must refuse every one.
`goParserRefuses` marks a rendersAnyway row the reader keeps only because
the two languages PARSE it differently, not because the legacy
tolerance resolves it. The offline writers' gate is allowed to
refuse those, and is asserted on every other rendersAnyway row.

storable.why: the unanchored field takes any https host
http is accepted by the same scheme rule every URL field applies
the apex itself is one of the bases
a subdomain of a base
http, which the write boundary accepts
Go lowercases the scheme it parses, so an uppercase one is storable
the write boundary trims before judging and stores the padded string, and the URL parser strips the same edges
Go folds U+0130 to ASCII and the browser punycodes it; the two name different accounts and both are under instagram.com
a subdomain of the first base
the second base, which is why facebook carries two
the pre-rebrand host
the post-rebrand host, which is why twitter carries two
a handle URL on the main host
YouTube's own share host, the second base
a subdomain of the first base
the web player, a subdomain of the base
the apex itself, which the backend base admits
the apex
the artist subdomain, which is how a Bandcamp account is spelled
the apex, which the social field admits even though the embed validator does not

storableButUnrenderable.why: a leading no-break space, which is what pasting a handle out of a rendered page produces: strings.TrimSpace strips it so the HTTP boundary stores it, while the URL parser keeps it and the value resolves to nothing. The offline writers' ValidateStoredSocialValue strips only what the parser strips, so it refuses this one
Go's parser takes any run of digits as a port; the WHATWG parser throws above 65535
Go treats xn-- as four ordinary bytes; the WHATWG parser decodes the label and throws when it does not decode

userinfo: the click does land on the platform, but it is attacker-chosen text that reads as a domain in a right-truncated status bar and that sameAs would publish inside an identity claim, so the reader refuses it as the release-link gate does

refusedByWriter.why: a foreign host wearing the platform's name
lookalike suffix, which the leading dot in the anchor exists to reject
prefix lookalike, rejected by the same dot
the platform name is in the query, which is what a substring check would have matched
userinfo spoofing the host; the hostname is evil.test in both parsers
not an http scheme, and the tolerance layer cannot produce one
the unanchored field is still held to the scheme rule
not an http scheme
a raw link-local address is not on the platform
U+3002 is a label separator to the browser's UTS-46 mapping, so the host resolves to instagram.com.evil.test
a trailing-dot host is neither equal to the base nor a subdomain of it, in either language
a redirector cannot be shown statically to land on-platform, so it is deliberately absent from the bases
lookalike suffix on the second-most-linked platform
bandcamp has no handle base, so a bare handle cannot resolve to an account
a scheme-less foreign domain, which the tolerance layer turns into a URL and the anchor then refuses
a legacy bare handle, which the handle base resolves onto instagram.com
a legacy bare handle with the @ prefix a social handle is written with
a real dotted handle from the dev seed: a dot alone must not make a handle look like a domain, or the seed stops loading
a dotted handle whose dots sit next to punctuation, also from the dev seed
a legacy scheme-less value already on the platform
a legacy bare handle
a legacy bare handle, which resolves onto the first base
a legacy bare handle
a legacy path fragment, which the handle base resolves onto the web player
a legacy bare handle
a legacy scheme-less value on the field that anchors no host
the domain shape test is case-insensitive, so this is repaired to a URL and refused rather than pasted onto the platform's base
protocol-relative: Go's parser reads no host at all and refuses, while the browser collapses the slashes and resolves the host, so the reader keeps it
neither a URL nor a handle: repairing it would produce https://123, which resolves to the host 0.0.0.123
Go's parser refuses a backslash in the authority; the browser folds it into the path, so the click still lands on instagram.com
